patch.value: Whole-workspace snapshot restore silently rewinds the immutable record: history streams are deleted and nothing records that a rewind happened

A workspace snapshot restore reverts item files and history streams to a content-addressed fingerprint. Measured on a sandbox tracker at build 2026.7.29: before the restore, two items and three history entries across two streams; after it, one item and one entry across one stream. The second item's entire history stream file was removed rather than tombstoned, the surviving item's update entry was erased, and no entry was written anywhere to say a restore occurred - not on any item stream and not on the workspace stream. History verify then reports a clean single-entry chain, so an observer arriving later sees a coherent, verifying record in which the erased work never existed. Every other destructive primitive in the product preserves proof: delete keeps the stream so point-in-time reads and per-item restore still answer, history-redact writes an audited redaction entry, history-compact writes a baseline entry that reconstructs correctly. Restore is also unguarded: no dry-run, no confirmation, no force flag on a whole-workspace revert, and an invalid target surfaces as an unhandled-error envelope. This is the residual of closed feature pm-dkrmzv, whose acceptance criteria covered atomicity, derived-state invalidation and lock safety but never the record of the revert itself.

A workspace restore appends a durable entry naming the snapshot fingerprint, the pre-restore workspace fingerprint, and the identity that ran it, and that entry survives the restore itself; Streams the restore reverts retain their erased entries in a form that keeps point-in-time reads answerable, or the restore refuses and names every stream it would truncate; The pre-restore state is captured so a restore is reversible, proven by a restore-then-return round trip that recovers every erased entry and every removed item; A whole-workspace revert requires an explicit confirmation or force flag and offers a dry-run reporting the item, stream, and entry counts it would remove; A conformance test asserts that no first-party command can reduce the entry count of an existing history stream without writing an audited record of the reduction
A whole-workspace revert is itself a recorded, reversible, guarded operation whose proof survives the revert.
Restore removes item files and their history streams and truncates surviving streams, leaving no audited entry and a history chain that verifies as if the erased work never existed.
